To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have generalized the 2-D turbulent Rhines scale to allow for depth-dependent flow and a finite deformation radius, and that this generalized Rhines scale predicts the latitudes of the observed vortices on Jupiter and Saturn.

(1) the Rhines scale for the cloud layer on Saturn is approximately 2.5° of longitude, (2) the latitudes of vortices correspond closely to the latitudes where the Rhines effect may be suppressed, and (3) this correspondence is consistent with the hypothesis that the Rhines effect is suppressed by a finite deformation radius.
the latitudes of vortices observed at Saturn are consistent with the latitudes predicted by the generalized Rhines scale.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamics of Jupiter and Saturn.
the interaction of Rossy waves with the turbulent flow in the upper atmosphere of Saturn.
the suppression of Rossby waves, and the formation and location of vortical structures in the atmosphere of Saturn.

“The Rhines effect is suppressed on Saturn at the same latitudes where vortices are observed, and the suppression of the Rhines scale may be responsible for the observed prevalence of vortical structures at these latitudes.”
the Rhines effect is suppressed in the cloud level on Saturn at the latitudes of the observed vortices.

the Rhines scale can be used to explain the latitudinal location of vorticity on Saturn. [2]
the Rhines scale, which is based on 2D turbulence theory and is a function of the zonal flow, is a useful tool in predicting the location of vorticities on Saturn.

the depth of the tropospheric deformation radius is an important factor to consider in the study of vortices, and that the depth of this deformation radius may vary with latitude.
Rossby wave suppression may be a general phenomenon in giant planets. [2]
